pack.title: Hidden in Plain Sight
pack.description: Sixteen boards of decoys, disguises and words hiding inside other words.

categories.title: ROOT VEGETABLES
categories.triviaFact: Carrots and parsnips belong to the same plant family as parsley, celery and fennel.

categories.title: PEOPLE IN SPY JARGON
categories.triviaFact: The novelist John le Carré helped popularize mole as the word for a spy hidden inside an organization.

categories.title: BURROWING ANIMALS
categories.triviaFact: A wombat's pouch faces backward, which helps keep soil out while the mother digs.

categories.title: BEFORE AGENT
categories.triviaFact: In professional sports, a free agent is a player who is out of contract and may sign with any team.

redHerrings.note: MOLE digs tunnels like WOMBAT and BADGER, but RABBIT, BADGER, WOMBAT and MEERKAT already complete the burrowers; MOLE is spy slang for an insider.
SLEEPER can precede AGENT, but LITERARY, TRAVEL, FREE and INSURANCE complete that set, while the spy jargon needs SLEEPER beside MOLE, HANDLER and ASSET.

categories.title: SOUNDS A DOG MAKES
categories.triviaFact: The basenji, a hunting dog from central Africa, is known for rarely barking and instead makes a yodel-like sound.

categories.title: PARTS OF A TREE
categories.triviaFact: Cork is harvested from the thick outer bark of the cork oak, which grows back after it has been stripped.

categories.title: GYMNASTICS APPARATUS
categories.triviaFact: The balance beam used in artistic gymnastics is only 10 centimeters wide.

categories.title: PLACES TO KEEP MONEY
categories.triviaFact: A till is the drawer where money is kept in a cash register, and in British English the word can mean the whole machine.

redHerrings.note: BARK is the most famous dog sound, but WOOF, YAP, GROWL and HOWL complete that set; BARK is also the outer layer of a tree.
Trees have growth RINGS, but BARK, ROOT, TWIG and LEAF already complete the tree; RINGS is a gymnastics apparatus.
VAULT is a gymnastics event, but BEAM, POMMEL HORSE, FLOOR and RINGS complete the apparatus; a bank VAULT keeps money.

categories.title: VERBS FOR HIDING SOMETHING
categories.triviaFact: Cache comes from the French verb cacher, meaning to conceal.

categories.title: ANIMAL COVERINGS
categories.triviaFact: Plumage, a bird's covering of feathers, comes from the French word plume, meaning feather.

categories.title: ANIMALS THAT CAN CHANGE COLOR
categories.triviaFact: Cuttlefish change color using chromatophores, elastic sacs of pigment that tiny muscles stretch open.

categories.title: FOLLOW TREASURE
categories.triviaFact: In English law, treasure trove once described hidden gold or silver whose owner could not be traced.

redHerrings.note: HIDE is the most obvious verb for hiding, but STASH, CACHE, BURY and CONCEAL complete that set; HIDE is also an animal's skin.
People bury treasure, but BURY comes before TREASURE rather than after it; it belongs with the hiding verbs.

categories.title: RACKET SPORTS
categories.triviaFact: Badminton takes its name from Badminton House, the Duke of Beaufort's country estate in Gloucestershire, England.

categories.title: PIZZA TOPPINGS
categories.triviaFact: Hawaiian pizza, topped with pineapple and ham, is usually credited to Sam Panopoulos, who served it in Canada in 1962.

categories.title: LAWMAKING TERMS
categories.triviaFact: Veto is Latin for I forbid, the word Roman tribunes used to block actions of magistrates or the Senate.

categories.title: END IN A COLOR
categories.triviaFact: The color amber is named after amber the gemstone, which is fossilized tree resin.

redHerrings.note: SAUSAGE is a classic pizza topping, but PEPPERONI, ANCHOVY, PINEAPPLE and ARTICHOKE complete that set; SAUSAGE ends in SAGE.
CHAMBER and IMPEACH sound like lawmaking words, but BILL, VETO, QUORUM and AMENDMENT complete that set; they end in AMBER and PEACH.

categories.title: CLOTHING FASTENERS
categories.triviaFact: A toggle is a short peg, often wooden, pushed through a loop, as on a traditional duffel coat.

categories.title: DRINKING ESTABLISHMENTS
categories.triviaFact: Pub is short for public house, the traditional British name for a place licensed to sell alcohol.

categories.title: INVENTORS
categories.triviaFact: Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867 and left most of his fortune to fund the Nobel Prizes.

categories.title: BEFORE CODE
categories.triviaFact: ZIP in the American ZIP Code stands for Zone Improvement Plan, a system introduced in 1963.

redHerrings.note: A ZIP fastens clothing, but BUTTON, BUCKLE, TOGGLE and CLASP complete that set; ZIP comes before CODE.
Samuel MORSE was an inventor, but EDISON, MARCONI, NOBEL and GUTENBERG complete that set; MORSE comes before CODE.
BAR can come before CODE, but ZIP, MORSE, DRESS and SOURCE complete that set; a BAR is a place to buy a drink, like a PUB or TAVERN.

categories.title: KINDS OF TOOTH
categories.triviaFact: An elephant's tusks are elongated incisor teeth that keep growing throughout its life.

categories.title: ADVERBS OF FREQUENCY
categories.triviaFact: In English, adverbs of frequency usually go before a main verb but after forms of the verb be.

categories.title: TYPES OF TRAIN
categories.triviaFact: Maglev, short for magnetic levitation, describes trains that hover above their guideway on magnetic fields.

categories.title: HIDE A NUMBER
categories.triviaFact: Canine comes from the Latin canis, meaning dog, while the nine hidden inside it goes back to Old English nigon.

redHerrings.note: CANINE is a kind of tooth, but MOLAR, INCISOR, FANG and TUSK complete that set; CANINE hides NINE.
OFTEN is an adverb of frequency, but SELDOM, ALWAYS, RARELY and USUALLY complete that set; OFTEN hides TEN.
A FREIGHT train is a type of train, but EXPRESS, MONORAIL, MAGLEV and COMMUTER complete that set; FREIGHT hides EIGHT.

categories.title: PLACES TO STAY
categories.triviaFact: The youth hostel movement began in Germany in 1909, inspired by the teacher Richard Schirrmann.

categories.title: ENTERTAINMENT AWARDS
categories.triviaFact: The Tony Awards are named after Antoinette Perry, an American actress, director and producer.

categories.title: SHAKESPEARE CHARACTERS
categories.triviaFact: Puck, the mischievous sprite in A Midsummer Night's Dream, is also called Robin Goodfellow.

categories.title: NATO PHONETIC ALPHABET WORDS
categories.triviaFact: The NATO phonetic alphabet gives each letter a code word so spellings stay clear over noisy radio links.

redHerrings.note: HOTEL is a place to stay, but HOSTEL, MOTEL, INN and GUESTHOUSE complete that set; HOTEL is the NATO word for H.
The OSCAR is a famous award, but EMMY, GRAMMY, TONY and BAFTA complete that set; OSCAR is the NATO word for O.
JULIET is also a NATO code word, officially spelled Juliett, but the Shakespeare set needs her beside OPHELIA, PUCK and PROSPERO.

categories.title: BITING INSECTS
categories.triviaFact: Only female horseflies bite, because they need protein from blood to develop their eggs.

categories.title: WEB BROWSERS
categories.triviaFact: Firefox grew out of the Mozilla project, and version 1.0 was released in November 2004.

categories.title: PARTS OF A CHURCH
categories.triviaFact: Nave comes from the Latin navis, meaning ship, which is also the root of the word navy.

categories.title: HIDE A CAPITAL CITY
categories.triviaFact: Quito, the capital of Ecuador, sits about 2,850 meters above sea level in the Andes.

redHerrings.note: MOSQUITO is the best-known biting insect, but MIDGE, FLEA, HORSEFLY and BEDBUG complete that set; MOSQUITO hides QUITO.
CHROME is a web browser, but FIREFOX, SAFARI, OPERA and EDGE complete that set; CHROME hides ROME.
PARISH sounds churchy, but it is a district rather than part of a church building; it hides PARIS.

categories.title: BREAKFAST FOODS
categories.triviaFact: Cereal takes its name from Ceres, the Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.

categories.title: VERBS FOR EATING
categories.triviaFact: Rodents gnaw constantly because their front incisor teeth never stop growing.

categories.title: POLICE RANKS
categories.triviaFact: Lieutenant comes from French words meaning place holder, for an officer who acts in a superior's place.

categories.title: PAINTER SURNAMES
categories.triviaFact: Edvard Munch made several versions of The Scream, including paintings, pastels and prints.

redHerrings.note: BACON is a breakfast food, but PORRIDGE, PANCAKE, CEREAL and OMELETTE complete that set; Francis BACON was a painter.
MUNCH means to eat, but CHEW, NIBBLE, GOBBLE and GNAW complete that set; Edvard MUNCH painted The Scream.
CONSTABLE is a police rank, but SERGEANT, INSPECTOR, LIEUTENANT and CAPTAIN complete that set; John CONSTABLE was a painter.
SERGEANT may recall the painter John Singer Sargent, but his name is spelled differently; SERGEANT is a police rank.

categories.title: FACIAL EXPRESSIONS
categories.triviaFact: A smile is produced mainly by the zygomatic major muscle, which pulls the corners of the mouth upward.

categories.title: WORDS FOR COWARDLY
categories.triviaFact: The sense of yellow meaning cowardly is recorded from the 1850s, though the reason for it is uncertain.

categories.title: OLD BRITISH COINS
categories.triviaFact: Before decimalization in 1971, a British pound was made up of 20 shillings.

categories.title: HIDE A BIRD
categories.triviaFact: The color teal takes its name from the common teal, a small duck with a stripe of similar color around its eye.

redHerrings.note: SCOWL is a facial expression, but FROWN, GRIN, SMIRK and POUT complete that set; SCOWL hides OWL.
CRAVEN means cowardly, but TIMID, GUTLESS, SPINELESS and YELLOW complete that set; CRAVEN hides RAVEN.
The CROWN was an old British coin worth five shillings, but FARTHING, SHILLING, FLORIN and GUINEA complete that set; CROWN hides CROW.

categories.title: CLASSIC BOARD GAMES
categories.triviaFact: Ludo is based on pachisi, a cross-and-circle board game that originated in India.

categories.title: CRIMES
categories.triviaFact: Arson comes from the Latin verb ardere, meaning to burn.

categories.title: SOCCER POSITIONS
categories.triviaFact: A sweeper, also called a libero, plays behind the back line to clear any ball that gets through.

categories.title: CONTAIN CONSECUTIVE LETTERS LIKE ABC
categories.triviaFact: Each of these words contains three letters that sit side by side in the alphabet, such as STU in student.

redHerrings.note: MONOPOLY is a classic board game, but SCRABBLE, RISK, LUDO and BACKGAMMON complete that set; MONOPOLY hides NOP.
To HIJACK is a crime, but FRAUD, ARSON, FORGERY and BRIBERY complete that set; HIJACK hides HIJ.
DEFENDER is a soccer position, but STRIKER, WINGER, GOALKEEPER and SWEEPER complete that set; DEFENDER begins with DEF.

categories.title: COFFEE DRINKS
categories.triviaFact: Latte is short for the Italian caffè latte, which simply means milk coffee.

categories.title: TYPES OF SWEATER
categories.triviaFact: The cardigan is named after James Brudenell, the 7th Earl of Cardigan, a British army officer.

categories.title: ISLANDS
categories.triviaFact: Java is the world's most populous island, home to more than half of Indonesia's population.

categories.title: PROGRAMMING LANGUAGES
categories.triviaFact: Python's creator, Guido van Rossum, named it after the comedy group Monty Python, not the snake.

redHerrings.note: JAVA is a programming language and slang for coffee, but PYTHON, RUBY, SWIFT and RUST complete the languages; JAVA is an Indonesian island.
In British English a JERSEY is a sweater, but CARDIGAN, PULLOVER, TURTLENECK and CREWNECK complete that set; JERSEY is a Channel Island.

categories.title: UNITS OF MASS
categories.triviaFact: A stone, still used in Britain and Ireland for body weight, equals 14 pounds, or about 6.35 kilograms.

categories.title: PLUMBING COMPONENTS
categories.triviaFact: A U-shaped trap under a sink holds water that stops sewer gases from rising into the room.

categories.title: ELEMENTS OF MUSIC
categories.triviaFact: Melody describes notes heard one after another, while harmony describes notes sounded together.

categories.title: SOUND LIKE VEGETABLES
categories.triviaFact: Swiss chard belongs to the same species as beetroot, but it is grown for its leaves rather than its root.

redHerrings.note: A CARAT is a unit of mass for gems, but GRAM, OUNCE, TONNE and STONE complete that set; CARAT sounds like carrot.
BEAT is a basic element of music, but RHYTHM, MELODY, HARMONY and TEMPO complete that set; BEAT sounds like beet.
A LEAK is a plumbing problem rather than a component like TAP, VALVE, PIPE or DRAIN; it sounds like leek.

categories.title: WINDOW COVERINGS
categories.triviaFact: Venetian blinds use horizontal slats that can be tilted to let in more or less light.

categories.title: CHESS TERMS
categories.triviaFact: Castling is the only chess move in which a player moves two pieces, the king and a rook, at once.

categories.title: WORDS FOR A CLIFF
categories.triviaFact: An escarpment is a long, steep slope that separates two areas of land at different heights.

categories.title: POKER TERMS
categories.triviaFact: In Texas hold'em, the river is the fifth and final community card dealt face up.

redHerrings.note: In poker a BLIND is a forced bet, but BLUFF, FLOP, TELL and RIVER complete the poker set; the window coverings need BLIND.
To CHECK is also a poker action, but the chess terms need it beside GAMBIT, CASTLING and STALEMATE.
A BLUFF is also a steep bank or cliff, but CRAG, PRECIPICE, ESCARPMENT and ROCK FACE complete that set; BLUFF is a poker term.

categories.title: HANDICRAFTS
categories.triviaFact: Crochet takes its name from the French word for a small hook, the tool used to make its stitches.

categories.title: OFFICE EQUIPMENT
categories.triviaFact: Cross-cut shredders slice paper into small pieces that are much harder to reassemble than long strips.

categories.title: ALLOYS
categories.triviaFact: Bronze is mainly copper and tin, while brass is mainly copper and zinc.

categories.title: TYPED ON THE TOP ROW OF A QWERTY KEYBOARD
categories.triviaFact: The QWERTY layout is named after the first six letters on the top row of letter keys.

redHerrings.note: A TYPEWRITER is classic office equipment, but STAPLER, SHREDDER, SCANNER and PRINTER complete that set; TYPEWRITER uses only top-row letters.
POTTERY is a handicraft, but KNITTING, WEAVING, CROCHET and QUILTING complete that set; POTTERY uses only top-row letters.
PEWTER is an alloy based on tin, but BRASS, BRONZE, STEEL and SOLDER complete that set; PEWTER uses only top-row letters.

categories.title: HORROR MOVIE MONSTERS
categories.triviaFact: Bram Stoker's 1897 novel Dracula did much to shape the modern image of the vampire.

categories.title: FABRICS
categories.triviaFact: Denim takes its name from serge de Nîmes, a sturdy fabric associated with the French city of Nîmes.

categories.title: BEFORE AID
categories.triviaFact: Legal aid helps people who cannot afford a lawyer to get free or low-cost advice and representation.

categories.title: LETTERS IN ALPHABETICAL ORDER
categories.triviaFact: Chintz, a glazed printed cotton, comes from the Hindi word chint, and its six letters run in alphabetical order.

redHerrings.note: A GHOST haunts many horror films, but VAMPIRE, ZOMBIE, MUMMY and WEREWOLF complete that set; G, H, O, S, T run in alphabetical order.
CHINTZ is a fabric, but DENIM, VELVET, TWEED and SATIN complete that set; its letters run in alphabetical order.
FIRST AID is the most familiar phrase, but LEGAL, HEARING, VISUAL and FOREIGN complete that set; F, I, R, S, T are in alphabetical order.
